newsitem.title: USA: PepsiCo leaves restaurants, looks overseas.
newsitem.headline: PepsiCo leaves restaurants, looks overseas.

text.p: After years of fighting shrinking returns in the crowded restaurant market, PepsiCo has decided to return to its roots -- soft drinks and snacks -- and meet rival Coca-Cola Co head-on overseas.

"There was a fundamental issue," PepsiCo chairman Roger Enrico said. "(Restaurants) are a retailing business and that introduced a level of complexity and a level of skills you really don't have in the package side. Restaurant and packaged goods are fundamentally different businesses with different dynmanics."

Enrico told a conference call with analysts that the company chose to spin off to shareholders the KFC, Taco Bell and Pizza Hut operations in a single company after "a great deal of reflection." PepsiCo's varied businesses were "not benefitting with a common corporate structure. The conclusion was we would be limiting ourselves on both sides" as a single corporation, he said.
Price wars and saturation of the domestic fast-food market with mushrooming outlets has stoked competition and pared margins, particularly in the last two years, analysts said.

Enrico emphasized that the new PepsiCo, expected to emerge by the end of the year, will be particularly focused on strengthening Pepsi-Cola sales outside of the United States, a market long considered Coke's big strength.

"We want to be aggressive on the international front. We are not going to catch Coke in Japan or Germany, but in places like China, India and Eastern Europe, there are billions of customers up for grabs and there is going to be a whole new story there," Enrico told the analysts.

Emmanuel Goldman, PepsiCo analyst at PaineWebber said there was room for both Coke and Pepsi in growing markets, "as long as Pepsi doesn't say 'We are going to take market share from Coke.' It is like trying to beat the Bulls in Chicago."
Wheat First Butcher Singer analyst John Maxwell agreed that the growth opportunities were overseas.

"Eighty-five percent of Coke's earnings come from outside the United States," he said. "PepsiCo is getting a little late to the party. They have to get in and fight and that will be done over five, 10 years, not one or two."
A PepsiCo spokesman said in 1995 the split between U.S. and international beverage revenues was 66 percent and 34 percent, respectively.

An international offensive would be well-financed, he added, since PepsiCo "will be flush with cash" after the spin-off because of an expected special dividend the restaurant company will pay to PepsiCo.
PepsiCo, in turn, will deliver the combined fast-food chains to shareholders debt-free. PepsiCo executives declined to say how large a dividend from the new company may be.
"People who hold PepsiCo debt took that debt with PepsiCo behind it and we are not going to change the game on them," Enrico said.
Maxwell said: "PepsiCo has about $9 billion in debt. Its hard to spin debt off to a new company, so they will get the new company to raise debt and and pay a dividend back to PepsiCo."
As for the bottom line, Roger Enrico indicated the kind if earnings growth rate he is looking for is 15 percent, Goldman said.
In 1992, the compounded annual earnings growth was 18.7 percent, according to Goldman, a typical rate before "all sorts of charges slowed it down."

"In 1993, PepsiCo made $1.00 per share and for 1996 we are projecting $1.24 per share, which implies a growth rate at about seven percent. It's an aberration in Pepsi's history and Enrico is looking to get the company back on the historic track," he added.

Of the new company, which will have annual revenue of more than $11 billion and 29,000 restaurants, Maxwell said: "The restaurants are top notch companies, but they have a lot of work to do. They have three of the top five concepts and are number one in Mexican, number one in pizza and number one in chicken. They said they were going to have to go back to basics, look at the menus."
Enrico also emphasized international opportunities for the eateries.

"The restaurants generated well over three-quarters of a billion dollars in cash and can continue expanding," he said. "We have doubled profits of the international restaurants in last two years. I think one day we will see more KFC restaurants in China than the United States."
According to a company spokesman, there are about 150 KFCs in China and about 5,000 in the United States.
Pepsico entered the restaurant business in 1977 with the purchase of Pizza Hut. Taco Bell was acquired in 1978, and KFC became part of Pepsico in 1986.
((-- Wall Street Desk, 212-859-1734)).
